utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Good morning to the technicians, the interpreters. Good morning to the members of the Prosecution, the members of the Defence, and all other persons present in the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Good morning, Mr. President. Case number IT-98-30-T. The Prosecutor versus Miroslav Kvocka, Milojica Kos, Mladjo Radic, and Zoran Zigic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I see we have some different members of the Prosecution team, so could we have the appearances, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Yes. My name is Niemann, and I appear with my colleagues, Ms. Hollis, Mr. Keegan, and Mr. Waidyaratnet, and Ms. Reynders is assisting the Prosecution. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Niemann. I turn now to the Defence. We have the same appearances as yesterday, but could you introduce yourself nevertheless, please? Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. With me this morning is Mr. Branko Lukic as co-counsel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. As yesterday, with me is Mrs. Jelena Nikolic and Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. The Defence of Mr. Radic is represented by Mr. Toma Fila and Zoran Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. The Defence of Zoran Zigic, as previously, is represented by Simo Tosic as lead counsel and Slobodan Stojanovic, an attorney from Belgrade, as co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. For today, it is envisaged that Mr. Kvocka should begin his testimony. So I give the floor to Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Before we begin with the examination-in-chief, on behalf of the entire Defence team, without analysing the opening statement of Mr. Niemann, I should like to express a protest. Mr. Niemann yesterday, in line 23, 24, page 5, declared that the Republika Srpska is a puppet entity. I must say that both in Dayton, and later in Paris, the Dayton Peace Agreement was signed in which the Republika Srpska is provided for as an entity, and today Bosnia-Herzegovina is functioning as a state of two equal entities, the Federation and the Republika Srpska. I'm sure that Mr. Niemann didn't mean his statement to be interpreted in the way we understood it. Let us consider it a rhetorical error rather than a position which would contest something that is verified by the International Community, because the greatest powers of the world are the granters of the Dayton Agreement. Through the functioning of Bosnia-Herzegovina and two equal entities, the desire is to ensure peace and stability. And we felt it necessary to draw attention to what we hope is an error in linguistics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Niemann, do you wish to react, or shall we close the incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, my comments were contemporaneous with the events, and I don't withdraw them, having regard to those times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it is not necessary to continue the discussion on this case because, after all, we are not here to have a discussion on that issue. We will close the incident, and we will begin with the testimony of Mr. Kvocka. Therefore, Mr. Simic, you have the floor for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I quite agree, Your Honour. Thank you. I should now like to call Mr. Kvocka to testify before this Tribunal, because we feel that his testimony can contribute significantly to the establishment of truth and to justice being served.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kvocka, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're going to read the solemn declaration that the usher will hand to you, Mr. Kvocka, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated, Mr. Kvocka. If you don't mind, Mr. Simic, before beginning this testimony. I should like to remind you, Mr. Kvocka, that you have just taken a solemn declaration saying that you will tell the truth, the whole truth. Therefore, you now enjoy the status of a witness. You are the accused, but now you are the witness, and therefore I wish to remind you that you are under the same obligations and duties as other witnesses. I should also like to remind you, because a certain confusion could occur, you come from a system in which the accused has the right to lie, to put it that way; however, I remind you that here you do not have that right. You are obliged to tell the truth, and you are under that obligation. So now you can testify, after I have reminded you of that obligation. Mr. Simic, it is now your turn to examine your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, the President has reminded you that you have to speak the truth. Let me also tell you that I am fully aware of the fact that some time has gone by since the events in question, that you have in the meantime reviewed the evidence produced by the Prosecution, and today you should tell us the things you know, perhaps things that you have heard, and at the same time to provide sources of information without entering into any polemics with the evidence produced by the Prosecutor. You tell us what you know and what you are familiar with. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. I shall do my best to act as you advise me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, when were you born?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I was born on January the 1st, 1957.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: In the village of Krivaja, Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: That close to the hamlet of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us the names of your parents?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: My father's name was Dragomir and my mother's Zdravka.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What were they by occupation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: My father was a worker, baker by occupation, by trade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Where did he work?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: He worked in a bakery.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: In view of the ethnic composition of the Prijedor municipality, was that bakery multi-ethnic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did your father have any problems in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Absolutely none.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What about your mother?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: My mother was a housewife.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: I apologise for going too fast. How many children did your parents have?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: My parents had five children.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: How many boys? How many girls?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: There were three brothers and two sisters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you go to school in the area of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Most of us except for me, or partially. I partially was educated in the area of Prijedor and partially further, beyond.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Upon the completion of your education, did you get married? Who did you marry?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I married Mrs. Jasminka Crnalic from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What is she by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: She is Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What were the names of your sisters?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Dragojla and Zorana.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What is the name of Zorana's husband?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: My sister Zorana's husband is called Halil Crnalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What is he by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: A Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Where are they living today?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: They are living in the United States of America.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: They are living there because in the course of these most unfortunate events that occurred in the former Yugoslavia, they had to flee from the area of Herzegovina where they used to live before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: That happened shortly after the war broke out in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So that means they've been living in the United States for some seven years?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did your father die in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: After your sister and her children left to the United States, did he have occasion to see them again?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No. We never saw one another again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Your mother never saw her daughter again either?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No, she did not either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Does your sister find this hard?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. She finds it very hard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And what about your mother?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, her situation is perhaps the worst. She finds it most difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And your sister Dragolja, you mentioned her too.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Whom did she marry?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: She was also married to a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And his name?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: For a moment I have forgotten because they divorced several years before the war, but I will remember perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, she has a child, doesn't she?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. She has a grown-up girl.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Were contacts broken off between the child and her father during the war?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: When did you start going out with your wife? Was there any resistance in your family against this relationship?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: In my family there was absolutely no resistance or reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was there any opposition or negative reactions on the part of your wife's family?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: When we started dating and going out there was a certain measure of opposition on the part of the parents of my wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: My wife's parents come from a very old conservative Prijedor family who attached great importance to religious principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Were these problems overcome?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: After we got married, me and Jasminka, those problems disappeared altogether. I was accepted by her family more or less as an equal member of the family.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Have you had children?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What sex?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: A girl and then a boy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What is the name of your daughter?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: My daughter's name is Sanela.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, is that a Muslim name?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. Absolutely a purely Muslim name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: You come from Omarska, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was Omarska virtually a hundred per cent populated by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, almost a hundred per cent, with two or three families belonging to other ethnic groups only.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: In spite of that situation, you gave your first child a Muslim name. Was that unusual?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: One could say it was unusual, but it was our decision. Actually, my wife and I discussed what name we would give our child, and my daughter [sic] wanted a Serb name, Mirjana, which she liked particularly, but I liked the name Sanela, and she conceded to me. But then our agreement was that when the second child came, my wife would choose the name for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: You had a son later on. What is his name?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Sinisa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Is that a Serbian name?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you get on well in your marriage with your wife?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. There were absolutely no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, I'm well aware of the troublesome period that you have lived through and you're still going through. Throughout this time, did you have the support of your wife?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. My wife supported me in every sense of the word. Especially now I find that support most encouraging, and it is very pronounced on her part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, in view of what you have been through and are going through now, you were often a subject in the media. Is it true that your wife, on one occasion and linked to your status at present, did she say that if she were to get married again a hundred times, she would marry Miroslav Kvocka again?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. This did happen, particularly on one occasion when there was more or less an offensive by the media against me when the indictment was published. She told a foreign journalist, a foreign reporter, that each and every time, if she were to marry again, she would marry Miroslav Kvocka, and I am most grateful to her for this. And as you have mentioned the media, maybe they will report this, and I have no other opportunity to thank her except in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Of course we will be discussing Omarska separately later on, but in the context of this subject, I should like to ask you how many brothers your sister had. I'm sorry, your wife. How many brothers did she have, your wife?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: My wife had a total of five brothers, but one brother, a few years prior to the war, died.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Let me now ask you a question regarding the location of your wife's brothers today?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Out of the four remaining brothers, three brothers are now in the United States of America.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And the fourth?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: And the fourth is in Sanski Most, which is part of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: How old is your mother-in-law?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I think she's close to 80. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Where is she today?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: She is also in America.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did they all have to leave as a consequence of the war?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. I would put it that way. The war and the consequences, the poverty, everything that followed resulted in their having to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And could we also say the insecurity?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. No one at the time could guarantee security 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: When they left, did they leave some considerable property behind?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, they left everything they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Has your wife seen her mother ever since she left to go to the States?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: In view of her age, the age of your mother-in-law, is it more or less certain that she will die without seeing her daughter and her grandchildren again?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: That is highly probable, in view of her age and ill-health.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that that is terrible?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: For our conditions and mentality and traditions, there is nothing worse than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Your wife and children, are they suffering as a result of this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Of course they are, in various ways. Of course, it is very difficult to describe in words how grandchildren suffer because their grandmother is away, and vice versa, and all the other things that this entails.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: You were working in the police.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, throughout my working lifetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: In view of the organisation of the police, it was organised on the basis of the so-called ethnic parity principle. Did you have colleagues who were Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, there were colleagues belonging to both ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And what were your relationships with them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Normal relationships, as among colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you have friends among them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Very close friends among my colleagues, policemen of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: For instance?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Just now, the names that come to mind are those who worked very closely with me, though there were others working further away, but those working with me were in Omarska: Edin Besic, Hamdija Arifagic, Fikret Harambasic, Emir Karabasic, and probably others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: These were your colleagues and friends; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, they were my friends and also colleagues from work, and also we were friends away from work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, in your family, in your upbringing, were you ever an extreme nationalist?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. I never agreed with that, nor did I pay very much attention to those matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Taking into account your life, I'm going to show you an exhibit that is a special exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Exhibit P14, Your Honours. This is a special type of exhibit whose contents are not part of the evidence, but rather it refers to a reaction or a response of Mr. Kvocka in a particular situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: -- do you recognise the book that is in your hands now?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: This is a Muslim religious book which is called the Koran.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What does it mean, in essence?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I believe that this is a basic book of Islamic religion, something similar to the Holy Bible that the Christians use, that is, the Orthodox.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: How do you know this book?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I came into possession of this book while I worked in Omarska, and I can describe how this came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: One of the detainees, a middle-aged man, was on the pista, and at one point, he sort of called me somewhat surreptitiously, and when I approached, he pulled out the book from his pocket and asked me if I could take it and give it to my wife or her parents, because he said that he knew them and that when everything was over, the investigation that he assumed that was going to take place, that they would have it in safekeeping and that he would pick it up from them once everything was over.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Taking into account the extreme views that prevailed at the time, could this book have been a source of trouble for that particular detainee?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that it could have. Had it been accidentally discovered by someone with extreme views, had this book been found on this man, it could have been a source of great trouble for this man. For a guard or anybody else who was found in possession of this book, in those times, this book would have been interpreted very badly. Immediately, this person would have been linked to the ideas promulgated in the book, and so on. In other words, he could have suffered consequences just by the fact of having possessed this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Could you have had problems, or could you have expected some negative response for what you did?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: In a nutshell, I could have fared the same way that he could have fared.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: By this act, did this person show a kind of confidence towards you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: This is how I can interpret it. Since he chose me, to hand it over to me, it means that he was not afraid of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What did you do with this book?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I left the book with my wife, and it has been in her possession until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you said that you came from a mixed marriage. In those ugly times, what was the attitude towards mixed marriages in general?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Sometime, I think it was as early as 1991, the opinions on mixed marriages deteriorated rapidly. So there were very negative attitudes which were publicly expressed by a number of people, including some very prominent ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you know of a statement by one of the founders of the HDZ, one of the nationalist parties in the area, who later became the President of Croatia, the late Franjo Tudjman, that he was happy that his wife was neither an ethnic Serb or a Jew?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. The media reported this to the public very widely, that is, this position of President Tudjman, that is, that expression of his views.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was this the position only of the Croatian leader, or was this opinion expressed in other communities as well?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: It was expressed among others as well. I remember, I read Dzemaludin Latic's views, who was one of the leaders of the SDA party, the Muslim party, from the founding, he said that mixed marriages were an unnatural thing, that it was an unnatural phenomenon, that it should stop, that it was just simply not natural. Also, certain Croatian priests referred to it as an unnatural thing, that is how they expressed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, was this position shared by some Serbian leaders?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Absolutely. You could read about it in the media. In one of the previous Status Conferences, a paragraph from the annex was adopted, the one offered by the Prosecution, this is from the judicial notice, and I think that the view expressed there was that children from the mixed marriages should be used for soap making.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: I think that the paragraph you were referring to is 344.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. I think you may be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: This is from the Prosecution's submission of 19 January, and it is part of the adjudicated facts in the case. However, you survived and you maintain your marriage.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: As far as the relationship between my wife and myself, our respective families, there was no response of any kind to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Have views of certain individuals changed with respect to your family? I will mention a case, a case from Omarska. We all know that a person by the name of Crnalic was killed in Omarska. He was the brother of a well-known handball player. Is it true that his brother, the handball player, and his sister have, regardless of that fact, actually maintained good relations with your family regardless of this? That they continued to visit you regularly while you were still free and that they continued to visit your wife to date?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. That is absolutely true there is a man named Crnalic, whose nickname is Roga. He was a well-known handball player. He continued to visit with my family and myself throughout these tragic events and continued to do so even after my arrest. His sister later has moved out of Prijedor, but she continues to come and visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And their brother was killed in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. He was killed at Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: In the context of your attitude towards these other ethnic groups, throughout this period were you and your wife the best man and maid of honour to another mixed marriage?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. I think this took place in 1994. I believe it could have been in May. I don't know the exact date, but this was on the occasion when we were witnesses, that is, the best man and maid of honour, to another mixed marriage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This, Your Honours, is Exhibit DP10.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I grant you this opportunity to say that this exhibit will have the number D2, and the previous one D1/1, and this is D2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. I apologise for interrupting you. Could you repeat, please, what you just said? We have some documents with certain numbers attached. Could you give us the exact correspondence between the documents that we have here on the numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid I don't have the exhibits, Mr. President, that you have. The first will be D1/1 and this exhibit will be D2/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a certain confusion may have arisen from the fact that we have numbered our own exhibits, and we were given an explanation from the registrar that he was going to number and register. So the number that I just called was the number which we used in our reference systems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Ms. Hollis, you wish to intervene?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Could we take this occasion to ask that a certain procedure be set regarding these exhibits and that we be allowed to look at the exhibit before it's provided to the witness so that we know what exhibit it is that they're being provided?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Is it possible to give a copy of these documents to the Prosecutor? In the case of the documents we have here at the bench, I don't know whether the Prosecutor has the same photocopies as we do, Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I have copies, but in light of the uncertainty of the numbers, if they would show us the exhibit, we could see which of our copies it is that they're talking about. We would like also like to look at this book because we've never seen that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, could you please assist? Mr. Simic, perhaps it would be appropriate to place the exhibits on the ELMO so that we can see what exhibit we are dealing with. Could that be done?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first of all, let me say that we have provided all exhibits to the Prosecution, that is, all the exhibits that we're going to present today and perhaps the next couple of days. They are all numbered and I will call each of these numbers. There is a technical possibility to follow this sequence. We can also put the exhibits on the ELMO, but we are facing technical problems. I am using the exhibits in the Serbian language, and we can provide copies of them to the usher and he can then use them as he wants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, it is important that we are all looking at the same document. So I suggest that you place the document under the ELMO, and then we can see whether it corresponds to what we have. So, Mr. Usher, will you please place under the ELMO this exhibit. Also, there's another reason. It is important for the public, who is following the proceedings, to be able to see the documents on the monitor as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I think we have squared things now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, who were these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, I apologise for interrupting you. Perhaps I'm going to ask the technical booth to give us an overview of the document so that we can see the number that the document bears. Is there a number on this document, please? Can it be focused in such a way that we can see the whole document with the number? Mr. Usher. Personally, I don't know which document this corresponds to in the pile that I have in front of me. So I understand the concerns of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the top-right corner --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting. There is a number 10 on this document circled in all piles, the piles for Judges and the piles for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have it now. But I do not see on the document that you have placed on the ELMO the number 10. So could you put the number on the document which you are placing on the ELMO? In that case, we can see immediately which document we are dealing with and we can match it up against what we have. So I think the objection of Ms. Hollis is quite correct, because we have to know and we must all know which document we are dealing with. So the document on the ELMO is rather hard to identify for us because it doesn't carry the number 10. If it has number 10 on the right-hand corner, then it is very easy to find it quickly. So perhaps we could now have a break and please deal with this question during the break, and we will resume after 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that we now have a code of communication between us all and that we can continue with our deliberations. Counsel Simic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. We have tendered the document, but we can't see it on the monitor, on the screen, as yet. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, may we continue?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, we may. I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: You have in front of you a copy of this document in English, but as you're well-acquainted with it, you can speak without the document, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: On what date did you and your wife testify, or were best man and maid of honour to a Muslim and a Serb in their marriage ceremony?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: This took place in May 1994, and I can see that it was exactly on the 12th of May, according to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What was the husband's name?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: The husband's name, my kum, was Hasan Oklopcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And the lady to whom he was married on the occasion?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Her name was Ljiljana Jesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, from the regions we come from, the institution of witness at a marriage ceremony, by tradition, is a very important event, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: According to custom, what term do we use to refer to these witnesses that witness the marriage between two people?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, in our country, in jargon, and generally the term used is the kum.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: By becoming a kum and setting up the whole kum relationship within a family, and by being witness to a marriage ceremony, what relationships are established between the people getting married and the people who serve as their kum?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, the relationships are very intimate, very close, ones of friendship, and the kum is almost equivalent, and in fact is equivalent to a brother. That is how close the relationship is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, by tradition, in the areas from which all of us come, is it customary for the kums and their children to enter into marriage?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Absolutely not. That is absolutely impossible by virtue of custom and tradition, and I do not know of any such cases, although there is nothing to stop them actually from doing so by law. But respecting the traditions and this relationship of kum, this is absolutely not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: When the marriage ceremony is completed, is there any custom to celebrate the event? Is that what happens?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, of course, that's what happens every time, and it is customary that there is a wedding ceremony and a wedding lunch. In times of peace, this is usually a very large wedding ceremony and lunch with lots of guests attending.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Is the wedding ceremony and lunch a public manifestation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: On the occasion, on this particular occasion, in view of your financial possibilities, did you have a wedding celebration of that kind?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Where was it held?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: We went to my flat, which is located in the Pecani settlement of Prijedor, and with some of our close friends and next-door neighbours and neighbours, we had a luncheon. We sat around and talked and generally celebrated the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: After that, did you continue to behave as befits a kum?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so. We had an intensive friendship going on. We would go swimming, to the beach, by the river bank in the summer. We would help each other, in view of the fact that there was no ready money to be had and it was very difficult to make a living.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you help your kum, Mr. Oklopcic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. I tried to do so whenever the occasion arose.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: How did you do this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, one way was that I helped him find a job, because he's an electrician by profession, and I did my best to find him a job, which lasted several months.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So did he work, and who did he work for?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. At my insistence and request, he worked with a well-known private entrepreneur, Vila Ranko, who was building a new facility, a printing press, in fact, and I called him up and asked him to employ my kum, to give my kum a job. He accepted this, although he didn't do so very readily because he was afraid of criticism, he was afraid of the extremists, and it was a little difficult for him to give this man a job. But I said that I would come to work with my kum, so that this would help me and help my kum. So he agreed in the end, and that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: At the job which was economically beneficial, were any other workers engaged?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. Several days later, another Muslim joined us -- his surname was Gecevic, I forget his name -- so that the three of us did the work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And was he an electrician as well?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, Gecevic is an electrician by profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And you had the role of helping them and covering them in their job?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, I'm a policeman, yes. I had nothing to do with the profession of electrician and the electrical trade, but I was there to see that everything went okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: After the work was completed and the job had been done, would you go to cafes where people could see you out with your kum?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, we did, because usually when your job is over, at the end of a day, we would go and have a drink, somewhere on our route home, and we used to do this too. We would mostly go to a cafe which was located in the marketplace at Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What was the proprietor's name of that cafe?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: The owner was called Nedzo, his name was Nedzo, and I forget his surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: The individual who was the proprietor of the cafe, did his brother -- was his brother killed in the war?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. That was common knowledge. On the door to the cafe, he would have the death certificate or obituary which testified to the death of his brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did this Mr. Nedzo have any criticisms to make, any objections to the fact that your kum and the other man, Gecevic, frequented his cafe?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, he did complain later on and said that he had a lot of complaints and pressure from his other guests who asked him how could he allow Muslims to sit in his cafe, and how could he allow Kvocka to bring Muslims to his cafe, whereas the Muslims had killed his brother a short while ago. So there was this difficult position for him, because he had this pressure and problems on the one side from other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you have any complaints, objections, pressure exerted on you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, at that time -- you mean during the time I was in the cafe? Well, no, not me personally. Not directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: May I ask you where your kums are now?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: My kums are now also in the United States of America. They went there quite recently. Before that they had been in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you still maintain contacts with them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Not as frequently, of course, in view of the situation, but last summer my kuma came to visit her relations in Prijedor and visited my family on that occasion too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did she bring your children presents?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, she did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did she express gratitude to you for your humane act and conduct in those difficult times?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, she did. They talked about the situation, and she thanked me for everything that we had done for her and for all our help. Quite simply, she could not understand what was going on in my particular position and with me, and that's what she told my wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, a moment ago you confirmed that the brother and sister would pay friendly visits to your house of the individual who was killed in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did your sister, whom, unfortunately, due to a tragedy that occurred in the areas from which we all come, after you were indicted and charged, did your sister have any problems in the United States; that is to say, her and her husband, did they have problems in the USA?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They also had pressure brought against them, and they were mistreated. At one point they even had to change the town in which they lived in. They had to move somewhere else where they would be less well known and where there were less emigres. So they were doubly mistreated. First, because they had a mixed marriage and, second, because I was an alleged war criminal, as they said, and things of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, as we are standing here and talking about your relationships towards other religious communities, when you worked in the police station at Tukovi, did you engage in any activity connected to the village of Alisici?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. There was a characteristic incident at the end of July and the beginning of August, I think it was. Anyway, it was in the summer, when my wife called me up from home and asked me to come home urgently because she needed some assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What kind of assistance did she need?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: When I came home, she told me, my wife, that is, told me that we had to go to the village of Alisici if that was at all possible. It was halfway between Prijedor and Sanski Most. That's where the village was located. It was in this village that my wife's family and my wife has close relations and other relations on her mother's side. They had called her, in the meantime, and told her that they were threatened there by great danger and that we should do whatever we could to save them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you undertake anything in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, I did. We tried to do whatever we could, although it was very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, because we had to find some oil, some petrol that we didn't have, and a driver who would be brave enough to make this undertaking, and to put them all into a truck and load up some things that they could take with them and bring them to Prijedor, to a safer place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you succeed in this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was able to find some petrol and a driver within the space of several hours. His name was Ignjatovic, his surname. We got into this truck, that is, the driver got into this truck and my wife and I took a passenger vehicle which was in Tukovi, at our disposal. In fact, I abused my official position there to avail myself of the vehicle. I went to the village of Alisici in front and the truck followed me behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: When you came to the village of Alisici, what did you find there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: In the village itself, you could hear various explosions and shooting, and close by you could see some houses smoking. The houses were on fire. They were ablaze. We came across my wife's family and their close relations, all in their house. There were quite a lot of them, not only the relations, and lots of other people as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Were they neighbours?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. They were the next-door neighbours mostly. They were very much afraid. They didn't know what to do. They saw that there was danger, and they asked us to help them in any way we could, to save them. Our close relation's name was Merdzic. He now lives somewhere in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What did you do in that situation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: We loaded up some of the things that they had already prepared up onto the truck, some clothes and food, and there were all these people there, and all of them got into a small truck, a two-tonne truck, which is what we call it -- it means it can take a lot of two tonnes -- and they sat in the truck underneath the tarpaulin, and we went towards Prijedor. Once again, my wife and I were in the car in front and they followed us behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Were there any explosions in the direction of the truck? Were you safe on your route?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No. We were not safe at all. As I said a moment ago, you could hear explosions all over the place. There was shooting nearby and of all this noise. We saw that the canopy -- the bullets had made holes in the canopy, but nobody was injured because I told everybody to lie down and keep down low in the truck. That is my police experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So you arrived in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. We arrived in Prijedor, but we had to pass through one or two checkpoints on our way to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What kind of checkpoints were they?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, they were police checkpoints, as far as I know. I don't know whether they were mixed army and police checkpoints, but I noticed policemen at the checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No, just Serbian. There were no Muslim checkpoints at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you have any unpleasantness at those checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, there was always unpleasantness, from simple provocations to the fact that they told me that I was saving Turks or, "You're saving Turks." Again, I apologise for that expression but that is the term they used.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Let us just clarify one point. The term "Turks," was that a derogatory term for the members of the Muslim community?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. At that time, when anybody said "Turks," then that was the a derogatory term that was used, because it is, of course, well known that it is not a purely Turkish population for them to actually be Turks, it was just derogatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So when you overcame all the obstacles and arrived in Prijedor, what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: We went to my mother-in-law's. She has a house in the centre of Prijedor, and all these people got out of the truck there and were accommodated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did they remain in your mother-in-law's house for any amount of time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They stayed there for quite a long time. I can't remember exactly how long, but they did stay for some considerable time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did your wife help these people by bringing food to her mother and food for the refugees as well?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, she did. She did this practically every day. She very often would prepare lunch for them in our flat and then came to get them and bring them over to lunch or she would take food over to them. But she did this every day, either one or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: We're going to go back to the question of what you mentioned, namely, that there were a lot of Muslims who were either relations or friends and that they came to your mother-in-law's house.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. As I said a moment ago, my wife's family is an old Muslim Prijedor family, highly respected, and it was a large family with many relations and, of course, many friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: One of the reasons for which the people went to your mother-in-law's house, was it the fact that you were her son-in-law and were a policeman? Was that one of the reasons?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: At that time, the motive -- they had even a greater motive to come. They expressed their desire to be there in her vicinity and, of course, near me as well by the same token. So this was a reason, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did this mean a certain amount of safety and protection for them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, that's how they felt. They felt safer, more secure, better protected. That is the feeling that they got.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, the other members of your family, for example, your sister Dragojla, who works in the court in Prijedor, in addition to the fact that she was married to a Muslim, did she have a broad circle of Muslim friends?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, she did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And judging by some of the photographs in your home, your sister with the president of the court of law, with Mr. Nedzad Salkic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I know for sure that we still have those photographs and many other photographs where you can see how my sister had many friends, amongst them Mr. Seric and some other Judges from Prijedor who were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: We'll go back to that question later on when we talk to your wife, because your wife has all the photographs in her possession. But tell me now, Mr. Kvocka, were you a member of the League of Communists?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was it customary that all policemen were members of the legal of communists?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, it was, almost 100 per cent. In the former Yugoslavia, all policemen were members of the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: In 1988, 1989, and 1990, it was becoming evident that communism was in for a fall. In our regions, new political ideas began to emerge. There was a multi-party system burgeoning. At that period, and we're talking about 1990 here, did you have any political affiliations or did you give political support to any of the new political programmes that were emerging?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, at that time, when there were manifest extreme nationalist ideas and parties, at that time, I found myself in a situation where I was not able to opt for any one of them. One particular party appeared and they called it the Reformists party or the Ante Markovic party and similar terms were used, and it was a sort of moderate party with a moderate approach as far as nationalism was concerned, and it propagated economic prosperity and development, managerial, entrepreneurial, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Now that you've mentioned the nationalist parties in the regions of the former Yugoslavia, could you tell us which were the three nationalist options that appeared in the course of 1990?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, the entire region was divided into three basic nationalist parties. They were the SDS, which was founded in Sarajevo; the SDA party, once again, founded in Sarajevo; and the HDZ party, and all the ethnic groups, according to their national structure -- ethnic structure, would join these different parties. I don't know what order they were actually established in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Let us make things a bit clearer. The SDS, whose party was that? What nationality did it belong to, what ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, the abbreviation "SDS" stood for the Serbian Democratic Party and was a party which was made up of exclusively Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What about the SDA party? Whose party was that, and what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: The SDA party was the party of the Muslim people founded by the Muslim extremist-oriented individuals, and it was composed almost exclusively of Muslims -- exclusively of Muslims, that is to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you recall a legal problem which arose with the foundation of the SDA party, difficulties over the law whether nationalistic parties could be founded and a decision of the law courts?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, it was common knowledge that when the Party of Democratic Action was founded, it obtained this name because it was supposed to be called the Muslim Democratic Party. However, the laws of the former Yugoslavia, which were still in force at the time, did not permit nationalistic names in the title. So that they had to alter the name from the Muslim Party to the Party of Democratic Action, the SDA party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And later on, did that law undergo any change, any amendments?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, later on, the title remained, but the law was probably changed because the Serbian Democratic Party could be registered under that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What about the HDZ party?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: The HDZ party is the Croatian Democratic Union, and the founders and members were exclusively Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: All those parties, in their name, include the attribute "democratic."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, in the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: This democratic attribute, was that the determinant, or was, rather, the nationalist attribute what determined the characteristics of the party?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: In my view, the national attribute was decisive, and this attribute "democratic" was simply a screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, you said that you supported the political concepts of the party headed by Mr. Ante Markovic, at the time, the prime minister. Did you do anything to take a more active part in that party?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: It was an idea that personally appealed to me most. In my town, there were several people who shared my views, and that circle of people mostly consisted of private entrepreneurs, because they viewed the party as offering a future for them. So we inquired, myself and a man called Timarac from Omarska, we went to Banja Luka to inquire about this party, and we spoke to a man called Miro Bjelic, I think his name was, who was the secretary for the Banja Luka branch of that party, or something like that. And so we inquired into the programme, the concept of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What is the occupation of the mentioned Timarac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Timarac is a caterer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Does he have his own restaurant today?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Until my arrest, he worked as a caterer, he had a cafe, and I think he still has it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: I know a long time has gone by since these events, but could you tell us the names of some of the leaders of the party headed by Mr. Ante Markovic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I shall try to recall the names of some of the better-known figures. For instance, from Banja Luka, a world-renowned handball player, Abaz Arslanagic, was interested in this principle and the concept upheld by that party. Also a well-known football player, Ivica Osim, who was later the team leader, he also opted for this party, and he advocated the ideas upheld by that party. Then Emir Kusturica, a well-known film director, a world-renowned director, wholeheartedly supported that party because he said that that was a party with a broad outlook and that he didn't need narrow-minded parties within which he couldn't live.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any instructions from Mr. Bjelic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelic told me that in Prijedor, too, there were several people who had an interest in this party and its programme and that we should contact them and talk to them and see what could be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did he mention a name?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: He mentioned the name of Marko Pavic, Milan Andzic, Nedzo Delic. Maybe some others, but I can't recall just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marko Pavic, is he the same gentleman who is now the communications minister in the government of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Marko Pavic is a minister in the current government of Republika Srpska. A moment ago when we were talking about Banja Luka, in addition to the names I mentioned, it was well-known that the current prime minister of Republika Srpska was one of the initiators for the founding of such a party for the region of Banja Luka, or maybe even further afield. I also remember hearing your name mentioned, though I didn't know you personally at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this. At least I can be sure that Mr. Niemann won't prosecute me. I'm just joking. Did Mr. Markovic have a promotion of his party in 1990, and where?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, in Prijedor. That year, a rally was held at Mount Kozara, a large popular rally as we describe it, which was attended by a very large number of people, and at this rally, he delivered a speech and presented the programme of his party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Can you assess the number of people attending that rally?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I know that in the media a large figure was mentioned, but this is a -- it is not a plateau, it is a mountain, so it is very difficult to judge how many people attended. But figures mentioned ranged between 20.000 and 30.000 to 100.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Were you there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you mentioned two very well-known names in the media. One is the name of Mr. Ivica Osim, a famous football player, a team manager of the Yugoslav National Team just before the war. What ethnicity was his wife, as the media wrote about this extensively?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I think she was Muslim, and he's a Croat, as we know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What about Mr. Abaz Arslanagic? Do you know what ethnicity his wife was?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. He was a Muslim, and his wife was a Serb from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, what was the attitude of these three parties that you named towards Mr. Markovic's party?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: One could hear, read everywhere that they did not recognise that party, that they simply denied it, persecuted it. They called it the party of mixed marriages, which was considered to be something derogatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ante Markovic, was he frequently described as an Ustasha by representatives of Serb extremists?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. By the Serbs, he was often referred to as an Ustasha.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And what does the term "Ustasha" stand for?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: The term "Ustasha" has been in use ever since the Second World War, and at the time, it denoted members of the most extremist units of Croats, of the Croatian army, who served the occupying force. They committed terrible crimes in the course of history, as you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did their activities affect the area of Prijedor too?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: The most pronounced form of Ustasha activities was the Jasenovac camp, which existed until the end of 1945. It was there throughout the Second World War, this Jasenovac camp, where Serbs, Jews and, I read from books, a few disobedient Croats too were detained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: How many kilometres is Jasenovac from Banja Luka, in relation to Dubica?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: If it is 35 kilometres from Prijedor, then it is 80 kilometres from Banja Luka. But if you take the Dubica road across Mount Kozara, then it is very close. I don't know exactly kilometre-wise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did a large number of citizens of Prijedor end up in Jasenovac, about which a film was made?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: An enormous number. Virtually all the men from the villages around Prijedor, and a part of the town of Prijedor, in this offensive, most of them ended up in Jasenovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: The political party of Mr. Markovic, did it succeed in growing roots in Prijedor and the surroundings, in establishing a foothold?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I think not really, except for the first initial attempts and that rally on Mount Kozara.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And why do you think that was so?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I think that what prevailed were the extremists. But let me say, also other nationalist forces did not support him. The SDA denied the value of such a party, and so did the HDZ, so that they were all against it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: After the parliamentary elections in November 1990, did that party and its leader, Ante Markovic, disappear from the political stage?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, they did, in my belief.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, who is a Croat, did he appear on the political scene of Croatia after those elections?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: He was not heard of again after the first multiparty elections. There was no mention of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, you said that nationalist parties had divided the people along ethnic lines.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: That the Serbs mostly supported the SDS; the Muslims, the SDA, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, that is exactly what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask the usher for his assistance to place two documents under the ELMO. My number is DP50. Could you place it under the ELMO, and one for the registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit D3/1 and D3/1A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, what was the previous number of the document, the document number 10?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was D2/1, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Ms. Hollis, for the moment, is the system functioning regarding the exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It is very helpful when Mr. Simic tells us the number he noted on the exhibit himself, which was 50, that enables us to find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Simic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, did you ever join or support the Serb option, that is, the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you ever talk to anyone from the party and express your wish to join?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No. I had no interest in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is evidence to show that Mr. Kvocka was never a member of the SDS party in view of his political views.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: I have a question for you, Mr. Kvocka, though it is a very private area that I'm touching upon, so it is up to you not to answer it if you'd rather not. Who did you vote for at the elections in November 1990?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I think it is not difficult to conclude from what I have said so far whom I voted for. As the elections were secret, I have no fear for voting for my option and according to my own conscience.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Yesterday Mr. Niemann spoke about the relationship of the SDS towards people who were not members of that party, so I should now like to ask you to take our Exhibit number 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, I know there's a problem and that is the following: These are not original documents, we were unable to obtain them, but the Prosecution has, and the Prosecution gave them to the Defence and the Defence will use them and comment on them as an exhibit, because indeed we could not get hold of those documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be Exhibit 4/1.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness said he didn't have the version in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you have before you a decision of the crisis staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, number 03-531/92, dated 22nd June 1992. In point one of this decision it is explicitly stated that all executive posts can be held exclusively by personnel of Serbian nationality. In paragraph two, it is particularly underlined that this applies to the Ministry of the Interior and the army. What is of the greatest importance for us is paragraph three which says and I quote: "Also, these posts cannot be held by persons of Serb ethnicity who did not confirm this by plebiscite or who have still not ideologically understood that the sole representative of the Serbian people is the Serbian Democratic Party." Were such positions made public in the media?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they were. In Official Gazettes too of the government at the time and also in the regular media.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did the Kozarski Vjesnik newspaper write about this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What did that mean in practice?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: What it meant was that the SDS proclaimed itself as the sole representative of the Serb people and as the sole leader of the Serb people, and those who were not in the SDS did not belong anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And such personnel policy, was it applied in practice?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. Following these decisions, all the managers were replaced and other officials in other bodies and in the enterprises.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was there any possibility, in 1992, for someone who did not have a membership card of the SDS to have any kind of leading position?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No, it was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was there mistrust towards people who were not members?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. There was a high degree of mistrust, and they simply refused to think about the possibility of somebody who was not a member of the SDS to hold a managerial post.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, was a similar ideology upheld by the other two parties, the SDA and the HDZ, when they were establishing their authority as a result of the election results in November 1990?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. Judging by what I read in the media in Prijedor, the SDA party had won at the elections, and they sought to appoint to the highest position their members and their cadres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So the principle was roughly the same.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. Absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: The SDS equals Serbs, the SDA equals Muslims, the HDZ equals Croats.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And those in between?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Those in between didn't belong anywhere, as if they didn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was this principle applied in the police force?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, it was. After the elections, appointments were made as a function of the election results.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: When the new authorities had been established and when you left Omarska -- we will be coming to that later in much greater detail, of course -- were there any deaths recorded among Muslims in Prijedor of natural causes, killings, or whatever?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, there were, after the establishment of the authorities and also later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: After you left Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Were there problems with funerals?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. There were many problems, because this was the period when the SDS or, rather, the Serbs took over power themselves. They took over all power in Prijedor by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Will you tell me who was the Hodza in Prijedor at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: The only Hodza who stayed on, because probably the others had left, was Solo Adil.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What is a Hodza?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: A Hodza is a Muslim religious leader or representative. The religious representative of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Can it be compared to a priest among the Serbs and Croats?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What were the problems linked to funerals then?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: At the time, it was very difficult to organise a funeral, be it a death of natural causes or as a result of killing, because the nationalists would not allow it. They simply wouldn't allow it. The people themselves, the Muslims, very often didn't even dare to try and bury their dead unless they had taken measures to protect themselves in some way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Solo, did he at the time ask for the assistance of the official authorities to assist him in the burial of the dead?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I think he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: On a number of occasions, did he request that you be a member of the security when those burials took place?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. He did that by asking for this, and on one occasion, with a relative of my wife, he came in person, together with this relative, to ask me, on a private basis, whether I would help them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Would you tell us where that funeral took place?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: The funeral was carried out in a suburb called Puharska in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So you attended that burial in order to provide security for the actual ceremony?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. I was the only Serb attending a Muslim funeral.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Before these tragic events, was it customary, either at Muslim or Serb or Croat funerals, representatives of all the peoples to attend depending on their relationship to the deceased, whether they were friends or acquaintances?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Before the nationalism became rampant and the nationalist parties appeared, it was customary in Prijedor for all people who knew the deceased or his family to attend the funeral regardless of the ethnic group they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So this was an expression of communal spirit.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. That was an expression of it before all these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you have any unpleasant experiences during any of these ceremonies for which you provided security?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. What happened is in respect of this funeral that I just mentioned in Puharska. The cemetery itself was at the intersection of the roads, and there was an improvised basketball field, and some young men, I say in their 20s, played, I think, pick-up basketball, and they created a lot of noise.
