It is well known that an Islamic funeral requires a certain amount of quiet and respect so that all the rituals, the prayers, and everything could be said. After several warnings, I managed to disperse that group, but I could easily have gotten into an altercation with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Were there any extreme reactions in terms of the burial itself?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: What do you mean, in general?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Any kind.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. Hasan Crnalic was told that he could not do this at all at that time in that place. His father-in-law died in the house and nobody dared to come to the house for two days. So Hasan Crnalic arrived two days later. I accompanied him so that he could make all the necessary preparations for a regular burial.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, those of us who have lived through this know that people lived through hardship, financial hardship.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. There were no salaries, no pensions, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was there any organised aid, assistance through charitable societies, Merhamet and the Circle of Serbian Sisters and things like that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. Such societies and such associations existed in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: The charity association Merhamet was part of what ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: The Muslim one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did they mostly provide assistance to the Muslim families throughout that difficult time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did the Merhamet association also provide assistance to your family?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: For a period of time they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Is there any record of this assistance?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. They had a list of the members of the association, and I believe that my wife has a membership card still.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did they enter the amounts and the date the assistance which they provided?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. I think that they put down dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you receive this assistance from the Merhamet association for two or three years following your engagement in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did they ask any questions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No. At first there were no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Prijedor is a relatively small town. People know each other. Did people in Prijedor know that for a period of time you worked at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. I think that practically all Muslims knew this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: This did not present an obstacle for the Merhamet association to continue providing assistance to your family?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No. I had a feeling that some of the workers there actually were glad to be able to assist me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Awhile ago, you mentioned that a number of Muslims that were housed in your mother-in-law's house. After the dissolution of the Omarska camp, did some of these people find assistance in your house?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Can you name any names?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. During the Omarska period and following that, as far as my mother-in-law's house is concerned, we mentioned the names of my relatives. As far as my apartment is concerned, a number of people took shelter there. I cannot recall everybody now, but there was a family, Sehic, a mother, father, son, and a daughter, they came. For a month they would come and spend the night if they felt that the situation in town was uncertain. Sometimes we would just go over to their apartment and bring them over.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: How about the Zelinkic [phoen] Family?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. The Zelinkic family stayed at my mother-in-law's a while later. See, I could not remember them right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Following your arrest, did Enver Zelinkic call from Sweden to provide assistance, to explain what type of person you were?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, she contacted my wife on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: On this occasion, did she say that her brother and her father did not dare speak because of the political situation but that she felt obliged to travel from Sweden to come and testify about what you did for her family?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. This is what she told my wife. She said that her brother and her brother's son, in fact, who spent the most time at my house were now residing in Kljuce, and the situation was such that they just did not dare report as witnesses because the local authorities there did not allow it and it would be dangerous for them, but since she was in Sweden, she felt that she ran no such risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have concluded an area of questioning, so perhaps this would be a good time for Mr. Kvocka to take a break, and if this is convenient for you, this may be a good time to take a break. We are now going to enter into areas which require a lot of concentration and focus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite so, Mr. Simic. It's quite convenient to have a break now. We had planned to do so around midday. So we're now going to have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, are we arriving at the Omarska camp? Will we be there shortly? You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid that we may not arrive there because we still have a number of questions that are of general character in order to get a better understanding of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is up to you to channel your examination-in-chief, but we are waiting. Please proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, are you ready?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: In order for all of us to gain a better understanding of the matter, we will very briefly touch on the town of Omarska itself in relation to Prijedor. Omarska is part of Prijedor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is part of the Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What is a municipality, administratively speaking?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: That is a certain territory which encompasses a certain area. It has its administrative authority, and it consists of the city of Prijedor and the local communes; that is, the administrative division into local communes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Were there municipal authorities in the territory of Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did the local commune of Omarska belong within the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Could you attempt to locate it geographically?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: The local commune of Omarska is about halfway between Banja Luka and Prijedor, several kilometres closer to Prijedor. In other words, it is about 25 kilometres from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: There is a highway, Banja Luka-Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Is this local commune by the highway or is it removed from it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: It is about 2 to 3 kilometres away from the main highway.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Could you try to tell us what is the square area of this local commune?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. But it's a very small area, if you only take into account the local commune of Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What about the hamlets that were made part of -- or the local villages that surrounded Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: If you take into account these surrounding local communes and villages, then it's a somewhat wider area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Organisationally speaking, the area of the local commune, do you know anything about the local administration of that local commune?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, you can say that there is an element of local authority, that is, that there is a link between the municipal authority and the local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Can you say what are the local institutions of power there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Institutionally speaking, there is a secretary for the local commune, and this is a technical position; then there are citizens assemblies; there is the president of the assembly, of this local commune; and a number of subordinate organs, I guess you can call them organs. This is in political terms. As far as other major features of the local communes are concerned, there is a health centre, a cultural centre; then there is a small detached police unit; there is a railroad station, several commercial stores, and one agriculture cooperative. And that's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Before the war, was there an agricultural enterprise which had its administrative seat there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Actually, no. There was a mining complex which was called Ljubija, that was the overall name, and it had a unit at Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did the Ljubija company have any business premises or any production facilities there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, there were some production facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What about any administrative buildings?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, there was an administration building which was part of the Ljubija Mining Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: How far was this industrial complex from the centre of the town and the police station?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: It was about 1.5 kilometres from the police station, and that was the centre of Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Territorially speaking, was the Ljubija mining complex part of the jurisdiction of the police station in Omarska? Did it have authority there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. From the security point of view, yes, it did belong to the jurisdiction of this police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: In other words, the police station was responsible for the security in that mining complex.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, to get closer to your employment at the police station in Omarska, I would first like to address an issue that I believe you are familiar with. The police force, at the time of your employment there, its official name was "Militia."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, until 1991 -- 1990/1991, it was called Militia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: In many documents, you will see the name "Militia," but we will use the term "police" or "police force," because this is the generally accepted name, in order for all of us to be able to better follow. You said that you are familiar with the police organisational structure.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with it. I know about -- in general terms, I know its overall organisation, and at the local level, I think I know it fairly well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: In the pertinent time, there were two levels of police operation; one was before the Serbs took over control of it and the second, after they took control of it. In regard to the first part, we will talk about the police force as it existed in, say, 1991. How was the police force organised?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Before the war, including 1991, in the territory of the entire Yugoslavia, there was a federal secretariat for internal affairs. This was the so-called federal SUP which was the overall authority for the entire Yugoslavia. Organisationally speaking, below this were the republican SUP organisations. In other words, every republic within the former Yugoslavia had its own secretariat for internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Let's address the organisation within a single republic. What was the mission of the federal secretariat, and what were the tasks of the republican secretariats?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: The federal secretariat controlled the police work for the entire country, that is, all of Yugoslavia, and it was superior to the republican secretariats. So the republican secretariat conducted all the police work within the territory of its republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did they submit bills regulating police work?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: In other words, we had the federal and republican laws governing police work.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, but they needed to be coordinated. The republican laws were always adopted on the basis of the federal ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, there was coordination, a system of coordination of regulations streaming down from the federal ones to the republican ones.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the police activities were strictly regulated by both the republican and federal regulations?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. There was a law of internal affairs, and there was a federal one and there were republican ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: On the basis of either the republican or federal laws, did the local ministries adopt their rules regulating their operation and other work?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. Especially the republican ones adopted their own rules for police operation and conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And these laws referred to the territory for which they were adopted.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And the regulations provided very strict rules of operation.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. All foreseeable incidents or events were covered by them, and the appropriate measures were also defined.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Let us now move to the practical implementation of these rules and regulations. As this was addressed previously by the Prosecution, it may be useful if we explain what changes took place on 31 December 1989.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: What year did you mention?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: That was 1989.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: In that year, the police in Bosnia-Herzegovina was reorganised. The so-called municipal SUP organisations, that is, secretariats for internal affairs, were dissolved, and they were replaced by public security stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What was the area of responsibility of a public security station?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: It covered the area of a single municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Now, we're still talking about 1989. With respect to the municipal secretariats for internal affairs, were there intermunicipal secretariats?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. Before this change, there was a secretariat for internal affairs which covered several municipalities, so you could call them regional secretariats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So this was a regional --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Principles?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. You mean these were based on regional principles and these were regional organs.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was this regional principle of organisation of police work kept?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, it was kept, but now it was replaced by the centre of public security.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What is the difference between a centre for public security and the former Intermunicipal Secretariat for Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, I personally didn't see any great difference in the organisational sense. Both the Centre for Public Security included a number of public security stations as did in previous times the regional secretariat. It also included a number of intermunicipal secretariats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, I see that you're a little tired. I'm asking you about the full name of the regional form of organisation for the police force. Is it a centre for public security or a public security station?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. It includes the centre for the security services, the centre for the security services.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So can we address it in the official form.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, I spent my whole life time working in the public security centre, so I find it difficult to assimilate this other name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to the municipal level for the time being. The service for public security, public security service, did that service exist in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: How was it divided up?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, it was divided into two departments, the service for public and the service for state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What did the State Security Service deal with?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: The State Security Service's job was exclusively related to state security matters and matters which were of interest to the security of the state, in the interests of protecting the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: You never worked in that service, did you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: The public security service. Let's take a look at that and what it was in charge of.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: The public security service had a number of spheres of activity, starting with some general administrative work such as issuing all types of documents, IDs, passports, and so on, right up to the police force as a department and the criminal service department, and their task was to prevent crime from taking place and to control traffic and ensure safety on the roads and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: You said that within the frameworks of the public security service we had the police service within it.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: How was that organised? In what way?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: In the public security stations there were police stations within them, within the public security stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: One or more police stations?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Depending.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What did it depend on?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, it depended on the size of the municipality, the number of inhabitants, the problems that the region had to deal with and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: If there were police stations, was there the legal possibility of founding some lower forms of police activity?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. Within the frameworks of the police stations, it was possible to organise police departments, depending, once again, on the structure of the area, the number of inhabitants, and so on. So that in the larger inhabited areas, larger settlements that came within the frameworks of the municipality, there were police departments of this kind as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: As you spent almost your entire lifetime working in Prijedor, could you please tell us what the organisation was like, whether there were a number of police stations, whether there were police departments within those police stations as well?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, on several occasions at different periods in the course of my work there, there was reorganisation within the police station of that kind, and it did come about that within the frameworks of a public security station, there were three or four police stations, and then these would be reduced to only one police station with three or four police departments within it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What is the difference between a police station and a police department?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: A police station is a basic organisational police unit which has its commander of the police station and his deputy --

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: No, I mean what different work did it do? What different work do they do?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: The police station covers a broader area, and within its composition it has these police departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: But what about the work they did and the competencies? Were there any differences there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, the difference was that a police station had far broader authorisation and competencies than a police precinct or department.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Is there any difference in territorial authority; that is to say, the territory that each was in charge of? Was there any difference there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so. There was a difference. The police department or precinct had its own territory, but this did not exclude the competence and the authority of the police station over that same territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: If I have understood you correctly, then that means that the police station, if it is one, it is in charge of the whole territory of the municipality. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, quite so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And the departments or precincts were only in charge of a narrower, smaller area of the general municipality area?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: You started saying something a moment ago, so let's go back to what you were going to embark upon with regard to the leadership of both these organisations. Who was in charge of the police station?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: The police station was led by the commander of the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did he have a deputy?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. There is always a deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Are there any other superior officials governing the work of the police station?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. There is one or more assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Why one or more?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, that depended, once again, on the problems and size of the area for which the police station was -- of which the police station was in charge. So there would be in some areas several assistants who would, each of them, have their own area of activity, of police activity. For example, public law and order. There would be one assistant in charge of public law and order. Crime would have another assistant, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: In that organisational structure, who has the supreme authority?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: The commander of the station issues orders, is the person who issues orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And the deputy commander and assistants, what do they do?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: They execute and implement the orders issued by the commander, komandir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: The police department or precinct, what is its command structure?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: In the department, there is just the commander or the leader of the department, and that is just one individual who is in command of the work of that department.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So there are no deputies or assistants?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No. In the police department, that kind of structure never existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: After the commander, komandir, if you have a certain number of policemen, is there any hierarchy as regards to the issuance of orders?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: If you're talking about the department, police department --

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No. In a police department there is only the commander, the leader, and the others are just ordinary policemen with no difference in rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, you mentioned the fact that during your work there were transformations. The police stations, police departments, all this was undergoing transformation. Now, did these transformations affect the Omarska station? Which we're going to focus on, of course.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, it did happen there. When I began working in Omarska in 1981 for the first time, it was called the police department.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Can you remember who the commander of the department was?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: The commander of that department at the time was Simo Miskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic, whom we mentioned as the president of the SDS when this unfortunate conflict came into being, is that the same one?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. Much later he retired, and after having retired, he became politically active.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: When did the department grow to become a station, a police station?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: This took place several years after I had started working. So if I start -- in 1981 there was a reorganisation and Omarska became a police station; that is to say, a police station was founded in Omarska. The department grew to become the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the command structure changed as well?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: The police station got a commander and a deputy commander and so on. Can you remember their names?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The commander of the station was Radovan Daljevic. The deputy commander was Dzuro Prpos, and the assistant was Miro Gavrilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And how did the situation evolve further?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, sometime in 1990, I think this coincided with the general organisation we were talking about a moment ago, and the police station at Omarska was abolished, and the departments, police department was revived. So it became once again the police department of Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And what happened to Mr. Daljevic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I think that he retired when this came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And what about Mr. Prpos?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Mr. Prpos moved to Prijedor, and I think he became the deputy commander in the traffics department of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What about Mr. Gavrilovic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Mr. Gavrilovic also moved to Prijedor to take up some other work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So now you only have a commander, komandir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. It was the only the commander of the department that remained and he was a new man.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Can you remember his name and surname?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: His name was Milutin Bujic [realtime transcript read in error "Buhic"].

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So we no longer had any deputies or assistants?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No. Those functions no longer existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Up until what time did Mr. Bujic perform the department commander?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Bujic was the commander of our department up until approximately the middle of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you worked in Omarska for a considerable length of time, do you know how many policemen worked in or should have -- was to work in the Omarska police department?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: An act called the "Systemisation of Work Posts," according to that document, this provided for 15 policemen, a total of 15 policemen. That is to say, 14 policemen and the commander of the department.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was this respected; that is to say, in 1992, did 15 policemen actually work in the department?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No. To all practical effects, we were always short three or four policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: In view of the events that were to follow and the names that we're going to mention fairly frequently, could you -- do you recall any policemen working in the department in 1992 prior to Mr. Bujic's departure?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I'll try to remember as many of the names as I can. In addition to myself in that department, there was Branislav Bojic who worked there; Ljuban Grahovac; Boro Delic, nicknamed Baja; Edin Besic, Hamdija Arifagic; Fikret Harambasic. I can't remember any more. Maybe I'll remember them later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. There seems to have been an error in the transcript. When speaking about the commander of the department, his name is Bujic. B-u-j-i-c is the correct spelling of that name. If that could be rectified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We're going to correct it, but perhaps, Mr. Simic, you could be of the greatest assistance to both the court reporters and the interpreters, who are not so familiar, perhaps, with all these names, and that would assist us too, if you could spell the names, to say B-u, et cetera. If you could spell the names, please, if possible. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall do our very best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I forgot to mention two other police then, Zeljko Meakic and Mlajo Radic. They too worked with me at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: In April 1992 --

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: I apologise once again. We seem to have a problem in the transcript. A very vital name has been left out, Zeljko Meakic, in front of Mlajo Radic. There was Zeljko Meakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that -- I don't see in the transcript what I heard in the translation. I think I heard the name Zeljko Meakic, and it should have come before Mladjo Radic, M-l-a-d-j-o; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has been corrected in the transcript. Thank you very much once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So the middle of April 1992 -- that's what we were talking about -- the post of commander was vacant. Which policeman wanted to become commander, komandir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: At the time, we began -- rumours had it that Bujic would no longer be commander in Omarska, and amongst the policemen themselves, there was considerable polemics, and it was thought that Branislav Bojic, Zeljko Meakic could replace him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Were there any formal conditions to be met, that is to say, which stipulated who could be a commander, who was qualified?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, by law, the commander of a department must have a higher education, which would be comparable to and in line with the police profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Within the schooling system of the former Yugoslavia, was there a higher school for internal affairs, or for the police force?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, there was, in a number of republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you attend the higher school for internal affairs?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Who became commander of the department in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: The commander became Zeljko Meakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did he have a deputy or an assistant?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: In addition to this professional composition of the police force, in the work of the police and, of course, the work of the departments, because that's what we're talking about at the moment, was there any reserve police formation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. In the overall system of the work of the police force, there was a reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Who was a reserve policeman?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, in principle, the reserve policemen could be people with the right positive traits that are required for a policeman; that is to say, that they were not criminals, that they had never been taken to court, that they were respected in the local community where they lived and worked, as the reserve police force was organised on a territorial basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we have misunderstood each other. What I wanted to ask you to explain was in what way could you become a reserve policeman? But I thank you for your explanations of what are the general traits of a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: One became a reserve policeman in the following manner: The public security station would have workers, clerks, in charge of this aspect, and there are plans for this in the public security stations. And it is according to those plans and in cooperation with the Defence Ministry that certain cadres are requested; that is to say, the Defence Ministry provides them and they then have to do service in the military police. And I think that that is the basic aspect of this matter, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: That means that they are conscripts then, does it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And within the frameworks of the legal provisions, they go and report to the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And the Ministry of Defence, via the municipal department, bearing in mind the existing plans and programmes, sends the individuals to one of the police stations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, that was the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And they become -- they are given the status of policeman.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: These policemen, when they arrived in the police force, were they trained at all?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: When was the reserve police force generally used?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: The reserve police force was generally used when there were certain major events taking place and when the police service, with its active policemen, was not able to do all the work. For example, when President Tito, in former times, used to come visiting, then a larger number of reserve policemen would be used to provide security and help the normal police force. This is also true in case of natural disasters, floods and so on, the reserve police force would be called upon to assist. Things of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What about the Olympics in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. When, in 1984, we had the winter Olympics in Sarajevo, practically all the reserve policemen were incorporated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, for security reasons, quite simply, because we had to cover a large area and physically ensure security and protection for the whole area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did a reserve policeman receive information at the Ministry of Defence as to which assignment he would be sent on?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, a reserve policeman would receive an assignment of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: As reserve policemen, were they given police uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was there any difference between the uniforms worn by the active policemen and the reserve police force?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: If we're talking about before the war, then there was a difference in the uniforms. They had a similar uniform but they would be of a slightly different colour, tone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: When a reserve policeman would be sent on an assignment, was he equated with the active policemen? Did he receive a salary during his work within the police force?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: If we're talking about before the war, then I think that their position was equal to the positions of the active policemen, yes. But before the war, he did not receive a separate salary, because if he was employed in a company, in an enterprise of whatever kind, he would receive his regular salary during the time that he was assigned to this reserve police work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did the state remunerate his company for the salary, for his absence in the company and his engagement by the police force?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, I assume that they did, but I didn't really have an insight into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: But theoretically speaking.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, theoretically speaking, it was that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What about in practice? What happened in practice, when somebody was sent on assignment, an active and a reserve policeman? Would an active policeman be assisted by a reserve policeman?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. What they tried to do was to ensure that the composition of a patrol, for example, would be conceived as you have described it, that there would be one or two reserve policemen attached to every active policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was there any reason for this type of organisation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, yes, there was. A reserve policeman, quite naturally, was not as professionally trained for police work as was the active policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What about these patrols and assignments? Did they have an educational aspect to them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. In addition to the fact that the active policemen were doing their regular duty in the area or on the ground, the active policemen were also there to train and teach the reserve policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And what was cooperation like? Was it always good?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: As far as I was able to note, and according to my experience, I always did have very proper and good cooperation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to how many reserve policemen the police department in Omarska had in the period we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: You mean April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Even before that.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Roughly, about 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, you spoke about the qualifications required for a policeman. Were any checks made among those people to see whether they had been convicted or not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, such checks were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So a person who had any convictions could not serve as a reserve policeman.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Under no circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Let us now go back to this hierarchy of control and command. You said that Mr. Meakic was the komandir or commander of the police station department.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Who was his superior?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: His immediate superior is the commander of the police station in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: As we are talking of the time when Mr. Meakic had already been appointed, do you know who was at that same time the police station commander in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: It was Dusan Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So Dusan Jankovic had a deputy and assistants, didn't he? Could you remember some of them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, I can. His deputy was Zilhad Hodzic, one of his assistants was Radovan Kecan, and he had more assistants, but I can't remember their names now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Who was the superior to Mr. Jankovic, if we're going from bottom upwards, along the hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: The superior of Mr. Jankovic was the chief of the public security station in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: In April 1992, before the takeover, who was that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Before the takeover, it was Hasan Talundzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Between Mr. Talundzic and Mr. Jankovic, was there another person who acted as the assistant for police to the head of the public security service?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: At that time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And according to the organisational chart, was such a position envisaged?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No, not at that time. Earlier on, such a position did exist, but when the transformations occurred that we have described, when municipal bodies were transformed into public security stations, then no such workplace existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So the SJB was part of the centre of the security services in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the next step in the hierarchy upwards was the head of the security services centre?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether at that level there was an assistant for police, an assistant chief for police, who had to coordinate the work of several public security stations?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. In the security centre, there was an entire section for the police which coordinated the work of the entire police force as part of that centre. But I cannot remember the name of the head of that section.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, when you say "the police," do you mean that you are referring to the coordination of the police stations and not the police force as such?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. The police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So let us go back again to the Omarska department of the police station, or any other, for that matter. You said that there was a komandir, a commander. How was the work of the other policemen organised?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: The other policemen had several types of duties. There was guard duty, patrol services or patrolling the territory, both terms were used; then there was also a type of duty called security. But in Omarska anyway, we had these three types of duties, three different jobs that policemen performed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was it clearly indicated which policeman was working on the security, which one was on duty, and which one was on patrol?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No, this was never defined with any precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Who made the plans in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: The daily plans were made by the department commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, any one of the policemen in that department could one day be on duty, another day be on patrol duty, and another day, he could be working on the security of a particular facility.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, it would happen like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: If you were working on holidays, were you given higher remuneration for those hours of work?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. There was a regulation which provided for compensation when workers were on duty on holidays, and that compensation was somewhat greater than normal working hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, again, with the help of the Prosecution, who seems to have done much of our work, we received two documents which we should like to tender, document 17/1 and 17/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, may I take this opportunity to ask Mr. Kvocka whether you are tired, whether you can continue. Do you need a break?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for your concern, Mr. President. I think I will manage to work until the end, as planned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't yet heard the whole translation. What was the answer of Mr. Kvocka? I didn't hear it. As we are going to conclude, as planned, at 2.30, my idea was to have perhaps a short break now, since we have interrupted anyway. We've been working for an hour, and we will have another hour, so perhaps we could have a 15-minute break for Mr. Kvocka to take a little rest. We'll have a 15-minute break now. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kvocka, do you feel better now, more rested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everything is fine, Your Honour. I was thinking of general fatigue, but as regards breaks, whenever you decide, we can have a break. Thank you for your concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you know, we're all tired. We're all working hard. It is now up to Mr. Simic to resume work. We have the documents, don't we?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. I have a problem. I can't hear the interpretation. Yes, I can hear now. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The technical people are always right, we used to say. So can you give us the number, first?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. We have received two documents. We received them just before the break. The document dated 7 January 1992 will have the number D5/1, and the other document will be D6/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. Registrar, but I have a document here which bears the number 7 for the Defence. What is the number of that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 17/1.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I now have the original documents. The document at your disposal, numbered 17/1, has been registered by the registrar as D5/1; and the document, the Serb version, 17/2, will now be Exhibit D6/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand now. But still, if there is a number on the Defence document, it is easier to give us the number for us to identify the document, and that is why I was looking for it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. President, but I myself didn't have the original, so I didn't know the exact numbers of those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any event, I think that we wanted to organise ourselves better to avoid wasting time and we're not managing to do that. I think, the registrar must have the same documents that we have here and which the Prosecutor has as well. We must all speak the same language when talking about documents. So for me, it is easier if somebody gives me a number of the document rather than the date of the document. So I'm asking the Defence, if possible, to give to the Prosecutor, to the Judges, and to the registrar, the same document so that we can speak the same language. So let's continue now, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The technical difficulties arose because we marked the Serbian version and not the English one, but we will remove that problem very shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, a moment ago we were talking about the way in which policemen were engaged and the duties they had within the framework of the police station, department, or precinct. You have before you a document on the assignments for the New Year holidays. Under number 56 -- could the documents be placed on the ELMO, please -- your name is mentioned. Miroslav Kvocka worked from the 1st of January 1992 to the 2nd, from 1500 until 0300 hours, and it says "touring" or "patrolling." Can you explain to the court what exactly you were doing then, and is that a duty assigned to regular active-duty policemen?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: That is a type of duty, policing duty that I described, and on these particular dates, together with another policeman, I was patrolling a certain area, a certain district which is within the jurisdiction of the Omarska police department.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So we're coming to a similar document but one that is very interesting to us. It is a report on work during the Mayday holidays, the 1st of May 1992. Under number 50, again -- number 50, please. Can we see it on the ELMO? We can see it now on the monitor. It says Kvocka Miroslav, 30th of April - 1st May, from 2200 to 0600, and it says "security." So this is another aspect of regular policing duties?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. This is one of those activities that the police engaged in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: I said that this document was of interest because of another topic that we're going to embark upon now, and that is the question of the takeover of power in Prijedor municipality. On the 30th of April 1992, power was taken over in Prijedor municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: As a policeman, did you have any knowledge that such an event would occur?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No, absolutely none. I had absolutely no information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: When did this takeover occur?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: On the 30th of April, in the early hours of the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: According to your regular assignments, can you remember what your work assignment was on the 30th of April or, rather, the -- I'm sorry, the eve of the takeover, on the eve of the takeover?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: If you're referring to the day prior to the 30th of April --

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I was working night duty as the policeman on duty in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So that is the night between the 29th and the 30th?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. The night between the 29th and the 30th of April, from 1900 on the 29th until 0700 on the 30th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So you were on duty in the police station in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, together with several other policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: In the course of the morning, by any form of communication, was the police station department of Omarska informed of the events that occurred on the 30th of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No. Until 0700, the time I spent in the premises of the police station in Omarska, I had no knowledge or information about it, nor did the two or three policemen who were on duty with me. We didn't discuss it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you receive news? Did anyone report to you, "Power has been taken over. There are new authorities in Omarska now"?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No. We had no information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Upon the completion of your shift, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I returned to Prijedor, to my family apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Your family or your wife and two children, did they spend that night in their apartment in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Like any other night?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: When did you learn that power had been taken over in Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: As soon as I entered my apartment. My wife had already heard some news reports about it on the radio, and then I too joined her in listening to these announcements broadcast on Radio Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What was the content of those announcements?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: They said -- this was in the form of a proclamation, announcing that in the early hours of the morning a takeover of power had been carried out by the Serbs or the Serb Democratic Party -- I'm not quite sure about that now -- that this had taken place in order, without a single bullet being fired, that the citizens should stay at home in peace, and that things would function normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Given your regular schedule, the shift schedules in Omarska police station, when were you supposed to again engage in your regular duties? Were there any changes there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. My next schedule was changed somewhat. According to the regular schedule of shifts, I was only supposed to report to duty the following day in the afternoon. However, the very next morning I received a call from commander Zeljko, and he told me that the schedule has been changed, that on that same day I needed to report to Omarska at 2200.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Is this the schedule which we have in front of us?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. That is the date, 30 April through 1 May, and the hours are 2200 to 0600.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who you were in the shift with?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I'm not exactly sure, but it is possible that Ljubo Grahovac, who is listed underneath, was also on that shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: In this report, it details that you were assigned to security. What were you assigned to? What specifically did you secure at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Zeljko Meakic was tasked with providing security for the most significant facilities in Omarska; in other words, that they needed to be covered in terms of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: From here, we can see that almost all police officers were involved in this. Was this increased security a direct consequence of the takeover of power and perhaps with the contingency of some trouble in mind?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. Usually these facilities were not secured to that extent, so now we were tasked with paying more attention to those.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Have I understood you correctly, that you did not have any knowledge about the takeover of power or any other activity which would fall outside of the usual scope of police activity at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I had no knowledge of any other activities relative to the takeover of power, and I did not know about it until, as I said, I listened to the radio reports on that with my wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: The takeover of power took place on the 30th of April, in the early morning hours. Did this takeover of power lead to any changes in your official duties or obligations, or to any of your colleagues' duties, for instance, like Mladjo Radic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So you continued to carry out the same duties.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. I had the exact same duties in the Omarska police station, and it continued that way; except for this change, that we had shorter breaks between the shifts in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: In other words, your time off was reduced.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: That is exactly the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: In other words, there was a certain pattern of duty time and time off. How long did it go on like that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I believe for a couple of days only. Then we returned to the original scheme.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Very well. You talked about the regular or active police force. Now, I'm not going to take you back to that, but in the months that followed, let's say two or three months hence, did the number of reserve police officers increase?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Could you give us an approximate number of how many reserve police officers were assigned to the police station?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: It is not easy to give the exact number because not all of them arrived at the same time. Sometimes several police officers would arrive in several intervals. But overall, 20 to 30 reserve police officers were engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Given the extraordinary situation that was in the field at the time, did you have any knowledge whether the old verification system, that is, the verification of the officers who were assigned to the police station, was still implemented?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that, but I know that these were very rapidly evolving events.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Since you are a police officer and you worked in that area, did you notice whether, among the reserve police officers, there were also individuals who, under normal circumstances, could not have been police officers?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: In other words, there were persons who had some problems in the past.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. I think that there were some among them who, under normal circumstances, would never have been employed as police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender the document marked 23.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This exhibit will be D7/1, and D7/1A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you have a public announcement before you. It is very short; I'm going to read it out. I think it reflects the situation very well. This announcement was issued by the crisis staff of the Prijedor municipality, and the text runs as follows: "The Crisis Staff of the Prijedor Municipality calls all men between 18 and 45 years of age, who are not serving either in the army or the police forces and have not been given war assignments yet, to report immediately to the Public Security Station in Prijedor regarding their service in the reserve police force on security duties. Failure to respond to this call implies legal sanctions." This call is addressed to the male population in the town of Prijedor. "In Prijedor, 2 June 1992. Secretariat for Information." Have you understood the contents of this announcement?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Is this in contravention to what you know about the regular police activity?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. I think you can see that no procedure was followed which was provided for in the regular times for police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was the crisis staff competent to replenish the police force with reserve forces?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Never before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: According to this document, everybody had to report to the police.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: That is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Those who did not have war assignments.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Everybody was supposed to report to the police station in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So does that mean that this was bypassing the criteria set out for the police officers in peacetime?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: You could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: In practice, following this announcement, were the reserve police forces increased, that is, in Prijedor or in the areas where you had available information?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: In practice, you could see that when you passed in the town. Let's say, going from home to work, you could see a lot of police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was this police activity a threat to the citizens, given the number of untrained and untested new officers?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: There was a risk of various incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you tell me now, could these people have been properly supplied with uniforms and everything else that would identify them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So does that mean that the police force was dressed differently, in different attire?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. You could notice that the police officers were wearing different combinations of uniforms, some parts of military uniforms, police uniforms, even civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, there was an increase in personnel more than normal, usual. There was a need for more weapons. Were all people armed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to the previous question. We talked about the regular procedures for replenishment of the reserve police force. You said that a reserve police officer would be issued a uniform. Would he typically be taking that uniform home with him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Normally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: When he would be issued a weapon, and we're talking about the previous times, the regular times, what happened in that case?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: He would be given a weapon when there was a need for him to be on duty. That is when he would be issued a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So that would mean that -- let's say a reserve police officer would show up at a police station, and the commander would issue him a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: This is the procedure from before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Very well. When he has finished his duty for the day, what would then happen? Or go to an exercise.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: After an exercise, let's say, he would clean the weapon and return it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: You mean return it to the police station?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Were these weapons stored in the police station? Was it under the control of the police?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes, it was in the police station, and in the precinct there was a room which was assigned for the so-called small arms, because these were only rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What type of weapon were reserve police officers typically issued?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: At the time when he would start his duty, if you are referring to the specific case when the weapons were turned over for a specific purpose, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: I think we did not understand each other. When I asked who -- what weapons the police officer was issued, I meant what kind of weapon.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: All policemen were issued automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And not pistols?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: When this large number of police officers was engaged, this -- let's say every police station or precinct had a set number of weapons that had been assigned to that particular station?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information from which sources these weapons were given the increased number of police officers? Where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I have no independent information about where they came from. I know that a number of them could not get it from the police precincts because there weren't enough weapons there, but I know that they were allowed to carry personal weapons, pistols, that is, if some members of the reserve police forces already owned or possessed a pistol legally. Then they were allowed to carry that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: To try to sum it up, the Omarska police station was only able to arm those police officers who were assigned them, according to the regular rules, as you put it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: The new reserve officers, were they trained at all?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: I believe that no special training was conducted, and I think that there was no time for it and no opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: I think that I'm almost done with this area, and I believe that we're also running out of time for today. As a police officer, could it happen that in the course of the night of the 30th of April, some conflicts or incidents could take place which would have threatened the safety and security of citizens, including your family which spent that night in your family apartment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Well, that is absolutely correct. Given the event, that is, the event that took place in Prijedor that night, this could have provoked a wider conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was it natural that contemplating this possibility, that you would have left your family unprotected in a town where such conflicts could have taken place?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: No, not at all. Had I known anything about what was going to happen that night, I would have made an effort to be as far away as possible from that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you have any friends who would have informed you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, my wife was angry with me. She said, "You're a police officer. You should have known what was going to happen. You could have taken us to a safer place."

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I had another area in mind which I was going to address before the key events at Omarska, and I was going to ask Mr. Kvocka to lay out for us his tasks and duties throughout his career, and this is what would sort of pave the way for the Omarska events. I don't know if you want me to start that now. It is something that will take some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. Simic. We obviously will not have the time today, but you will have it tomorrow, because I think it would not be right to cut in half pieces of this testimony which constitute a whole. So I think we shall adjourn now, and we will resume tomorrow, tomorrow morning at 9.30. I can see that Mr. Niemann has something to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Tomorrow morning I'm in another matter, and I won't be available now for the rest of the two-week period. So may I have Your Honours' leave to be absent for that time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But we'll have other representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Of course. My colleague, Ms. Hollis, will certainly take over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. I think I see Mr. Tosic also, who has something to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my apologies for addressing you now. I was just trying to find the right moment during the day to request assistance in solving a problem that my client Zoran Zigic has. This morning when he was transported, apparently one security guard was putting handcuffs on his hands, and they leave -- they were placed on him too tightly. So it's very uncomfortable. The entire trip from the detention unit to the court building he suffered discomfort. Even though he asked for the handcuffs to be loosened, his request was ignored by the security personnel, which caused my client some anguish. I would like to ask for the Tribunal's assistance in order for this not to be repeated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, you will take note of this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Immediately after the hearing, I shall contact the competent people to see what actually happened and then to take follow-up measures in response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, we will monitor the situation, and the registrar will report to us, and we will take the necessary measures. I think that is all for today. We'll be meeting again tomorrow at 9.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: 2.30 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 1st day of March, 2000 at 9.30 a.m. 23 24 25
